title: NJ cops deliver lunch after arresting DoorDash driver - NewsBreak
text:
By Jen Ursillo ,
2 hours ago Washington Twp. (Gloucester County) police deliver a DoorDash order to a customer after arresting the driver for having outstanding warrants (Washington Twp. PD via Facebook) 🚔 DoorDash driver arrested mid-delivery in Washington Twp
🍔 NJ cops step in to complete food order themselves
📱 Police Facebook post turns unexpected bust into viral moment WASHINGTON TWP — What was supposed to be a simple DoorDash delivery turned into something a little more complicated, and totally unexpected for one New Jersey woman.
DoorDash driver arrested in Washington Township traffic stop On March 1, around noon, two officers from the Washington Township, Gloucester County Police Department pulled over a vehicle in front of the high school for a traffic violation.
ALSO READ: NJ beach house bookings are exploding for 2026 Washington Twp. (Gloucester County) police deliver a DoorDash order to a customer after arresting the driver for having outstanding warrants (Washington Twp. PD via Facebook) They soon discovered the driver was a wanted person with outstanding warrants .
While being placed under arrest, officials said the driver informed the cops he was in the middle of making a DoorDash delivery right up the block from where he got pulled over.
Washington Twp. (Gloucester County) police deliver a DoorDash order to a customer after arresting the driver for having outstanding warrants (Washington Twp. PD via Facebook) NJ police officers deliver DoorDash order themselves No problem.
Washington Township Police Department Officer Mike Scheer and Sgt. Matt Barnett made sure the customer got her DoorDash order by delivering it themselves, before the vehicle was towed.
Washington Township police Facebook post draws laughs “Teamwork makes dreamwork. And to the resident who answered the door, we are sorry for the surprise and for startling you. We hope lunch was still hot,” the department jokingly wrote on its Facebook page .
11 ways New Jersey is making it harder for ICE to operate With 12,000 additional officers, Immigration and Customs Enforcement wants to ramp up detention efforts this year. In New Jersey, proposed measures have been rolled out at the local, county, state and federal levels. Here's a look at what supporters have proposed as safeguards against unconstitutional actions — and what critics call hindrances to immigration enforcement. Gallery Credit: Erin Vogt Tero Vesalainen NJ asks residents to submit video of ICE agents A new website run by the state Attorney General’s Office lets residents submit video/photos of potentially concerning ICE activities directly to the state.
"Federal agents have authority to enforce federal immigration laws, but they must do so lawfully," the Attorney General's website says . "Examples of concerning activity include uses of excessive force, warrantless searches or arrests, racial profiling, wrongful detentions, interference with voting, or other civil-rights violations."
While it is not a crime to videorecord law enforcement as long as the person is not interfering, critics of this project say it encourages people to get in the way of federal agents as they conduct their jobs. (Getty Stock, Lawrey) No more face masks on ICE agents This proposed state measure — A1743/S3112 — would restrict ICE agents from wearing full-face masks during raids in New Jersey, a practice that many have likened to "secret police" in repressive regimes. Those who defend the ICE practice say the masks are necessary because agents and their families have faced threats (which is already illegal).
The measure also would require law enforcement officers to present sufficient identification prior to arresting or detaining a person.
An officer would be exempt when on an undercover assignment or other tactical operation, including violent-crime or organized-crime suppression. There are also exceptions for "threat of retaliation" and wearing masks to guard against illness or extreme weather. (Getty Stock, ThinkStock) Banning hospital and MVC cooperation with ICE Proposed bill A4070 would restrict the collection and sharing of certain personal information by state and local government entities and health care facilities.
It would also ban motor vehicle records from being shared without a person's informed consent, a signed warrant, lawful court order, or a subpoena, except when it would be contrary to federal law. (Getty Stock, ThinkStock) Making 'sanctuary state' policies offical law Proposed Bill A4071 /S3521 would codify the state Attorney General's Immigrant Trust Directive, which critics said made New Jersey a "sanctuary state" under then-Gov. Phil Murphy.
Under the bill, a law enforcement officer would be restricted from engaging in "racially-influenced policing."
The law would also make it illegal to stop, question, search, or detain any individual based solely on actual or suspected citizenship or immigration status or actual or suspected violations of federal civil immigration law.
Just as with the directive in place since 2018 , the law would not apply to accused criminals. Delaney Hall in Newark (Google Maps) Impose a hefty tax on for-profit detention centers Bill A4300 would create a 50% tax on the gross receipts of private detention facilities operating in New Jersey.
The legislation would direct proceeds into a new "Immigrant Protection Fund" dedicated to immigration services for New Jersey residents.
In July 2025, the Third Circuit Court of Appeals rejected key parts of the state’s ban on privately run immigrant detention centers.
According to ICE, a “Detention Reengineering Initiative” planned nationwide call for eight “large-scale detention centers,” each housing up to 10,000 detainees for up to 60 days each.
ICE is also securing 16 “processing sites” this year, includind a Roxbury warehouse site , prompting bipartisan objections within the town and neighboring Parsippany -Troy Hills. Investigate ICE officers As proposed by state lawmakers, Bill A4301 would authorize all state, county, and municipal law enforcement officers to access crime scenes and evidence within their jurisdiction.
The measure would make it a criminal offense for any person, including a federal officer, to block that access. One of the sponsors, Assemblywoman Katie Brennan, D-Hudson, said it is in reaction to situations such as in Minneapolis, following ICE encounters. Banning ICE agents from public employment Bill A4302 would disqualify ICE agents and officers who serve from Sept. 1, 2025, to Jan. 20, 2029, from holding future employment as state or local government employees, law enforcement officers, or teachers in New Jersey.
Assemblywoman Katie Brennan, D-Hudson, said "lawlessness on behalf of current ICE agents should eliminate them from serving in other public roles around the state."
Brennan and fellow Hudson County Assemblyman Ravi Bhalla joined Assemblywomen Annette Quijano and Alixon Collazos-Gill as prime sponsors of these bills. State Sen. Raj Mukherji, D-Hudson, will introduce the same measures in the state Senate. Getty Images/iStockphoto Jersey City bans ICE on municipal property On Jan. 23, Jersey City Mayor James Solomon issued an executive order that prohibits city property from being used for immigration raids.
"To every immigrant resident: You belong here. This is your home. And this city will fight for you,” Solomon said. He added that more than 40% of the city’s residents were born in a foreign country.
Solomon took the action after ICE raids around the state in Morristown , Princeton and Red Bank. (Canva, Townsquare Media Illustration) Hudson County bans ICE on county property Hudson County Executive Craig Guy, a Democrat, signed an executive order on Jan. 30 that prohibits federal immigration authorities , including ICE and Customs and Border Protection, from any civil immigration enforcement activities within Hudson County-owned, leased, or operated buildings, unless required by law or under a valid warrant.
It is similar to the order signed by Jersey City Mayor James Solomon. Banning ICE arrests at Homeland Security offices U.S. Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, D-N.J. 12th District, introduced a measure to ban ICE arrests at Homeland Security field offices.
The federal bill would stop the arrest of anyone arriving or leaving a Homeland Security field office for immigration review. Photo via Kathleen Gail Stopping ICE agents from hiding their license plates The Protecting License-plate Access for Transparency and Enforcement Act, or PLATE Act, would ban federal immigration officers from hiding or manipulating license plates on their vehicles.
It was introduced by U.S. Rep. Nelli Pou, D-N.J. 9th District. attachment-attachment-delaney-hall-detention-facility-in-newark
